prophecies.title: Does Isaiah 7:14 predict the virgin birth of Jesus?
prophecies.claim: Isaiah said a virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, 'God with us'. Matthew 1:22-23 says this was fulfilled when Mary conceived Jesus without a man. Many Christians grant the sign had a first meaning for King Ahaz but say its full meaning is Jesus, the only child who is literally God with us.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The sign is given to King Ahaz of Judah while two kings are attacking Jerusalem (Isaiah 7:1-2). The Hebrew says הָעַלְמָה (hāʿalmāh), 'the young woman', and describes her as הָרָה (hārāh), 'pregnant'; the usual Hebrew word for virgin, בְּתוּלָה (bᵉtūlāh, as in Genesis 24:16), is not used. Verse 16 gives the time limit: before the child knows right from wrong, the land of the two enemy kings will be deserted, which points to Ahaz's own lifetime. Matthew quotes the old Greek translation (the Septuagint), which has παρθένος (parthenos), 'virgin'. The name Immanuel comes back in Isaiah 8:8 and 8:10 in the same Assyrian crisis.

other_readings.reading: The child is one born in Ahaz's own time. Rashi says the young woman is Isaiah's own wife; others have said Ahaz's wife and her son Hezekiah. A birth seven centuries later could not be a sign to Ahaz, and the Hebrew word does not mean virgin.

The Quran teaches that Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin (Quran 19:20, Quran 3:47), so Muslims accept the virgin birth without relying on Isaiah. They do not accept that 'God with us' makes Jesus divine.
Most see a sign fulfilled in the 730s BCE, when Assyria crushed Damascus and northern Israel, and treat Matthew's use as a later re-reading through the Greek translation.

prophecies.status_reason: The passage sets its own deadline in the time of Ahaz, and the Hebrew word means young woman, not virgin. The link to Jesus depends on the Greek translation and on reading a second, later meaning into the verse.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading fits the Hebrew and the context better; the Christian reading works only as a second, deeper meaning that the passage itself does not state.

prophecies.title: Does Isaiah 9:6 call the Messiah 'Mighty God'?
prophecies.claim: Isaiah foretells a child who will sit on David's throne and be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Christians say no merely human king can carry the name 'Mighty God', and that only Jesus, a son of David whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32-33), fits. Matthew 4:14-16 applies the opening of the same passage to Jesus.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: In Hebrew Bibles these are verses 5 and 6 of chapter 9. The child is given the name פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ אֵל גִּבּוֹר אֲבִי־עַד שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם (peleʾ yōʿēts ʾēl gibbōr ʾăvī-ʿad sar-shālōm). אֵל גִּבּוֹר (ʾēl gibbōr), 'mighty God', is used of God himself in Isaiah 10:21. The verbs are in the past form ('a child has been born to us'), and verse 7 promises endless peace and a rule 'on David's throne' from then on forever. The New Testament never quotes verse 6 itself about Jesus.

other_readings.reading: Rashi reads the long name as a sentence about God: the Wonderful Counselor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, called the child 'Prince of Peace'. He and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 94a) apply it to King Hezekiah, already born when Isaiah spoke. Hebrew names often praise God without making the bearer God, as Immanuel does.
A human being cannot be God or God's son; the Quran calls Jesus a messenger only (Quran 5:75). If the verse is about the Messiah, the titles honour God who sent him.
Usually read as a poem for the birth or crowning of a Davidic king in Isaiah's day, using lofty throne-names of the kind kings in the region were given.

prophecies.status_reason: The text does give a Davidic child a name containing 'Mighty God', which is the strongest point for the Christian reading. But the grammar allows the name to be a statement about God, the verbs look back on a birth already past, and the endless peace on David's throne in verse 7 has not been seen.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: Evenly balanced on the name itself; the timing and the unfulfilled peace of verse 7 favour the Jewish reading.

prophecies.title: Is the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 Jesus?
prophecies.claim: Isaiah describes a servant who is despised, pierced for the sins of others, silent like a lamb led to slaughter, killed, buried with a rich man, and then sees the fruit of his suffering. Christians say this is the clearest picture of the crucifixion in the Hebrew Bible, written centuries before it happened. Philip preaches Jesus from this very passage in Acts 8:32-35, and 1 Peter 2:24 quotes 'by his wounds you were healed'.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The passage speaks of עַבְדִּי (ʿavdī), 'my servant', as a single 'he' who suffers for 'our' sins: he is מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ (mᵉḥōlāl mippᵉshāʿēnū), 'pierced' or 'wounded because of our transgressions' (53:5), is 'cut off from the land of the living' (53:8) and is given a grave. It also says he 'will see offspring' and 'prolong his days' (53:10). The servant is never named in this chapter. In the chapters around it God calls Israel 'my servant' (Isaiah 41:8, 44:1, 49:3), yet in Isaiah 49:6 the servant has a mission to restore Israel, so he is also pictured as distinct from the nation.

other_readings.reading: Rashi and most later commentators say the servant is Israel, or the righteous within Israel, whose suffering in exile astonishes the nations who speak in 53:1-9. Ibn Ezra objects that Jesus did not 'see offspring' or 'prolong his days'. Older Jewish sources did read it of the Messiah: Targum Jonathan renders 52:13 'my servant the Messiah', and Sanhedrin 98b applies 53:4 to him.
The Quran says Jesus was not killed or crucified (Quran 4:157) and that no soul bears another's burden (Quran 6:164), so a Messiah dying for others' sins is rejected.
Divided between Israel as a whole, a faithful group within Israel, and an individual such as the prophet himself.

prophecies.status_reason: The text describes one who suffers and dies for the sins of others and is then vindicated, which matches the Christian account closely. But it does not name him, the surrounding chapters call Israel the servant, and 'see offspring' and 'prolong his days' fit Jesus only if read figuratively or of resurrection.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: Evenly balanced: the wording of chapter 53 suits an individual who dies for others, while the surrounding chapters support Israel.

prophecies.title: Does Psalm 22 describe the crucifixion?
prophecies.claim: David wrote 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?', 'they pierced my hands and my feet' and 'they cast lots for my clothing' about a thousand years before Jesus. Jesus cried the first line on the cross (Matthew 27:46) and soldiers gambled for his clothes (John 19:24). Christians say no event in David's own life matches, and crucifixion had not yet been invented.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The psalm is a first-person prayer of a suffering man, not framed as a prediction. He is mocked, surrounded by enemies pictured as bulls, lions and dogs, his clothes are divided by lot (22:18), and from 22:21 onward he is rescued and praises God in the assembly. In the traditional Hebrew text (verse 17 in Hebrew numbering) the key word is כָּאֲרִי (kāʾărī), 'like a lion [at] my hands and feet'; the old Greek translation has ὤρυξαν (ōryxan), 'they dug'. 'Pierced' comes from the Greek and from a variant Hebrew spelling. No New Testament writer quotes the 'pierced' line.

other_readings.reading: A psalm of David about his own distress, or about Israel in exile. Rashi reads 'like a lion, my hands and feet', as if mauled by a lion, comparing Isaiah 38:13. The psalm ends with rescue, not death.

The Quran denies that Jesus was crucified (Quran 4:157), so the psalm cannot be a prophecy of his crucifixion. Some Muslims add that the speaker is saved in the end (22:21-24), as they believe Jesus was.
An individual lament of a common type. The Gospel writers told the crucifixion in the words of this psalm, so the matches partly reflect how the story was told.

prophecies.status_reason: The cry of abandonment, the mocking and the dividing of clothes do match the Gospel accounts. But the psalm is a prayer, not a prediction, the 'pierced' reading is textually disputed, and the sufferer is delivered rather than killed.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading matches what kind of text this is; the Christian reading rests on real parallels but treats a prayer as a forecast.

prophecies.title: Does Micah 5:2 predict the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem?
prophecies.claim: Micah names Bethlehem as the place the future ruler of Israel will come from, and says his origins are 'from of old, from everlasting'. Jesus was born in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5-6, Luke 2:4). Christians add that 'from everlasting' shows the ruler existed before his birth.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: In Hebrew Bibles this is verse 1 of chapter 5. It says that from Bethlehem Ephrathah, David's home town, will come 'one who is to be ruler in Israel', מוֹשֵׁל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (mōshēl bᵉyisrāʾēl). His origins are מִקֶּדֶם מִימֵי עוֹלָם (miqqedem mīmē ʿōlām), 'from of old, from ancient days'; the same phrase 'days of old' in Micah 7:14 means the distant past, not eternity. The verses that follow say he will shepherd Israel in security, be great to the ends of the earth, and deliver the land from Assyria (5:4-6).

other_readings.reading: Rashi agrees this is the Messiah, son of David, and takes Bethlehem as the place David's line comes from. The ruler must actually rule Israel and bring it security, which Jesus did not do. 'From ancient days' points to the ancient house of David.
Muslims accept Jesus as the Messiah but not as an eternal being; 'from ancient days' is read as ancient lineage. Ruling Israel is not something the Quran says Jesus did in his first life on earth.

A hope for a new David from David's clan. Many note that Matthew and Luke explain the family's presence in Bethlehem in different ways, and that John 7:42 shows the Bethlehem expectation was already well known.

prophecies.status_reason: The text clearly expects a ruler from Bethlehem, and the Gospels place Jesus's birth there. But the same sentence says he will rule Israel and the next verses say he will give it peace and safety from its enemies, which did not happen in his lifetime; 'from everlasting' is a stronger translation than the Hebrew requires.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: Evenly balanced: the birthplace fits the Christian claim, the ruling and the peace fit the Jewish objection that it is not yet fulfilled.

prophecies.title: Did Jesus fulfil Zechariah 9:9 by riding a donkey into Jerusalem?
prophecies.claim: Zechariah said Jerusalem's king would come humble and riding on a donkey. Jesus entered Jerusalem exactly this way, and both Matthew 21:4-5 and John 12:14-15 say it fulfilled the prophecy. Christians say the humble arrival shows a Messiah who comes first in lowliness before he comes in power.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: Verse 9 pictures Zion's king arriving צַדִּיק וְנוֹשָׁע (tsaddīq wᵉnōshāʿ), 'righteous and saved' or 'victorious', and עָנִי (ʿānī), 'humble' or 'afflicted', riding a donkey. Verse 10 continues the same sentence: chariots, war horses and battle bows are removed, he speaks peace to the nations, and his rule runs 'from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth'. The text does not separate the arrival from the worldwide peace.

other_readings.reading: The passage is about the Messiah, but its two verses belong together: the king on the donkey is the king who ends war and rules the world. Since war did not end, the prophecy is still waiting.
Muslims accept Jesus as the Messiah and have no objection to the entry into Jerusalem, but hold that worldwide rule and peace did not come through him at that time.
Riding a donkey is an act a person can choose to perform, and the Gospels present Jesus as arranging it; it shows a claim being made rather than an outcome outside his control.

prophecies.status_reason: Verse 9 matches the Gospel story, but riding a donkey is something a person can do on purpose, and verse 10, the end of war and worldwide rule, has not happened. Christians place verse 10 at a second coming, which the passage does not mention.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading keeps verses 9 and 10 together as the text does; the Christian reading matches verse 9 and postpones verse 10.

prophecies.title: Does Zechariah 12:10 say God himself will be pierced?
prophecies.claim: God says, 'they will look to me whom they have pierced'. Christians say that here God speaks of himself as pierced, which only makes sense if the pierced Jesus is God. John 19:37 quotes the verse at the crucifixion, and Revelation 1:7 says every eye will see him, including those who pierced him.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: God is the speaker, promising to defend Jerusalem against the nations (12:9) and to pour out a spirit of grace on the house of David. The Hebrew reads וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דָּקָרוּ (wᵉhibbīṭū ʾēlay ʾēt ʾăsher dāqārū), literally 'they will look to me, the one whom they pierced', and then switches person: 'and they will mourn for him as for an only son'. The switch from 'me' to 'him' is the difficulty. John 19:37 quotes it as 'him whom they pierced', not 'me'.

other_readings.reading: Rashi: they will look to God and lament over those among them whom the nations pierced and killed. The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) records another view, that the mourning is for the Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed in the final war. Either way the pierced one is a human being, not God.
God cannot be pierced or die, and the Quran denies that Jesus was killed (Quran 4:157). The verse is read as mourning for someone slain in a future battle.
The Hebrew is awkward and may be damaged. Many translate 'they will look to me concerning the one they pierced', a slain figure whose identity is unknown.

prophecies.status_reason: The Hebrew does have 'to me' next to 'whom they pierced', and an early rabbinic view even links the verse to a slain Messiah. But the next words mourn for 'him', a different person from the speaker, and the New Testament itself quotes it as 'him'. The setting is a future siege of Jerusalem in which the people of Jerusalem repent.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: Evenly balanced on a pierced messianic figure; the claim that God himself is the one pierced goes beyond what the grammar can prove.

prophecies.title: Do Daniel's seventy weeks point to the date of Jesus's death?
prophecies.claim: Daniel was told that 69 'weeks' of years, 483 years, would run from the order to rebuild Jerusalem to the Messiah, who would then be 'cut off', and that afterwards the city and temple would be destroyed. Counting from the decree in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:7, about 458 BCE) reaches about 26 CE, the start of Jesus's ministry. Jesus was killed a few years later and Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 70 CE, so the Messiah had to come before then.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: Seventy שָׁבֻעִים (shāvuʿīm), 'weeks' or 'sevens', are decreed for Daniel's people and city. Verse 25 counts 'seven weeks and sixty-two weeks' to מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד (māshīaḥ nāgīd), 'an anointed one, a leader'; there is no 'the' in Hebrew, and 'anointed' is used of priests (Leviticus 4:3) and of Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1). The traditional Hebrew punctuation puts a break after 'seven weeks', giving one anointed leader after 7 weeks and another anointed one 'cut off' after a further 62; the King James Version joins the numbers into 69. After that, a coming leader's people destroy the city and sanctuary, and sacrifice stops for half a week.

other_readings.reading: Rashi takes the first anointed one as Cyrus and the one cut off as King Agrippa, with Titus destroying the temple. The periods are counted from the first temple's destruction to the second's. The word is 'an anointed one', not 'the Messiah'.
There is no standard Muslim reading of this passage. The Quran calls Jesus the Messiah but denies that he was killed (Quran 4:157), so a Messiah who is 'cut off' by death is not accepted.

Most date the fulfilment to the second century BCE: the anointed one cut off is the high priest Onias III, killed about 171 BCE, and the half-week without sacrifice is the persecution under Antiochus IV in 167-164 BCE.

prophecies.status_reason: The passage really does speak of an anointed one being cut off before the city and sanctuary are destroyed, and one way of counting lands close to Jesus's time. But the result depends on which starting decree is chosen, on joining the 7 and 62 weeks against the Hebrew punctuation, and on reading 'an anointed one' as 'the Messiah'.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: Evenly balanced: the order of events suits the Christian reading, but the arithmetic only works with choices the text does not make for the reader.

prophecies.title: Is 'Out of Egypt I called my son' a prophecy about Jesus?
prophecies.claim: Hosea wrote 'out of Egypt I called my son'. Matthew 2:15 says this was fulfilled when the child Jesus was taken to Egypt and brought back. Christians say Jesus relives Israel's story as God's true Son, so what was said of Israel finds its full meaning in him.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The whole verse reads כִּי נַעַר יִשְׂרָאֵל וָאֹהֲבֵהוּ וּמִמִּצְרַיִם קָרָאתִי לִבְנִי (kī naʿar yisrāʾēl wāʾōhăvēhū ūmimmitsrayim qārāʾtī livnī), 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son'. The son is named: Israel. The verbs are past, looking back to the Exodus, where God calls Israel 'my son, my firstborn' (Exodus 4:22). The next verse says this son went on to sacrifice to the Baals. Nothing in the passage looks forward to a future person.

other_readings.reading: A plain statement about the Exodus, not a prediction. Rashi reads on into the next verse: God called his son, and Israel turned away. It cannot be about a sinless Messiah.
The verse is about the Children of Israel leaving Egypt under Moses. Calling Israel God's 'son' shows the word is a figure of speech for a loved people, not a literal sonship.
Matthew uses typology: he presents Jesus as repeating Israel's history. That is a way of interpreting, not evidence that Hosea predicted anything.

prophecies.status_reason: As a prediction it fails: the verse is a past-tense statement that names Israel as the son and goes on to describe that son's idolatry. Matthew's use works only as a pattern (Jesus as a new Israel), which is a theological comparison, not a fulfilled forecast.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading is what the text says; the Christian reading is a symbolic re-use of it.

prophecies.title: Did Jesus bring the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31?
prophecies.claim: Jeremiah promised a new covenant, unlike the one made at the Exodus, with sins forgiven and God's law written on the heart. At the Last Supper Jesus said, 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20). Hebrews 8:8-13 quotes Jeremiah in full and concludes that the first covenant is now old and passing away.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: God promises בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה (bᵉrīt ḥădāshāh), 'a new covenant', and says who it is with: 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah'. What is new is where the law is kept: 'I will put my law (תּוֹרָתִי, tōrātī) in their inward parts and write it on their heart'. The law itself is not said to be replaced. The result is that nobody will need to teach his neighbour to know God, 'for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest', and their sin will be forgiven.

other_readings.reading: The same Torah, renewed and kept from the heart, for a reunited Israel and Judah restored to their land. It has not happened yet: people still have to be taught to know God. Nothing in the passage says the commandments end or that the covenant passes to another people.

Covenants with earlier communities were real but were broken, and God's final guidance came through Muhammad. The Quran also speaks of its message being brought down upon the Prophet's heart (Quran 26:192-194).
A promise of inner renewal for the exiles of both kingdoms. The first Christians applied the phrase to their own movement.

prophecies.status_reason: The phrase 'new covenant' is Jeremiah's, and forgiveness of sins is part of it, which supports the Christian claim. But the covenant is made with Israel and Judah, it writes the existing Torah on the heart rather than setting it aside, and the state where no one needs teaching has not arrived.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading follows the wording more closely; the Christian reading takes up the promise but changes who it is with and what happens to the law.

prophecies.title: Is the 'prophet like Moses' in Deuteronomy 18:18 Muhammad?
prophecies.claim: God told Moses he would raise up a prophet like him from among the Israelites' 'brothers' and put his words in his mouth. Muslims say the brothers of Israel are the Ishmaelites, and that Muhammad is like Moses in ways Jesus is not: born naturally, married with children, a lawgiver, a ruler and commander who died a natural death. 'I will put my words in his mouth' fits a prophet who recited what he heard, and the Quran says he is found in the Torah (Quran 7:157) and compares him to the messenger sent to Pharaoh (Quran 73:15).
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The key phrase is מִקֶּרֶב אֲחֵיהֶם (miqqerev ʾăḥēhem), 'from among their brothers'. Three verses earlier Moses says the same thing to Israel as 'from among you, of your brothers' (18:15). The same phrase in Deuteronomy 17:15 means an Israelite: the king must be 'from among your brothers', 'not a foreigner'. Deuteronomy does once call the descendants of Esau 'your brothers' (2:4), so the word can reach beyond Israel, but 'from among you' in 18:15 narrows it here. The setting is a promise that Israel will have prophets in the land instead of the fortune-tellers of the nations, with a test for false prophets (18:20-22).

other_readings.reading: A promise of a line of prophets from within Israel after Moses, beginning with Joshua, not one single future figure. Deuteronomy 34:10 adds that no prophet as great as Moses arose again in Israel.

Peter applies the verse to Jesus in Acts 3:22-23, and John 5:46 has Jesus say Moses wrote about him. Jesus was an Israelite, 'from among you', and like Moses mediated a covenant and spoke God's words.
The passage sets up the office of prophet in Israel. Later Jews did expect one final 'prophet' (John 1:21), but still an Israelite one.

prophecies.status_reason: The likenesses between Moses and Muhammad are real, but the text says 'from among you, of your brothers', and Deuteronomy uses that exact wording for fellow Israelites as opposed to foreigners. The Ishmaelite reading has to set aside verse 15.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish and Christian reading that the prophet is an Israelite fits the wording better; which Israelite is a separate question the verse does not settle.

prophecies.title: Does Deuteronomy 33:2 foretell Moses, Jesus and Muhammad?
prophecies.claim: Moses said the Lord came from Sinai, rose from Seir and shone from Mount Paran, with ten thousand holy ones and a fiery law in his right hand. Muslims read this as three revelations: the Torah at Sinai, the Gospel in the land of Seir, and the Quran in Paran, where Ishmael lived (Genesis 21:21) and which they identify with the region of Mecca. The 'ten thousand holy ones' are matched with the ten thousand companions who entered Mecca with Muhammad, and the 'fiery law' with the sharia.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: This is the opening of Moses's blessing on the tribes of Israel before his death (33:1). The verbs are past: יְהוָה מִסִּינַי בָּא (YHWH missīnay bāʾ), 'the LORD came from Sinai', 'rose from Seir', 'shone from Mount Paran'. The one who comes is God, not a prophet, and he comes 'to them', to Israel. Seir and Paran are regions on Israel's desert route south of Canaan: Israel moved from the wilderness of Sinai to the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 10:12), and Habakkuk 3:3 uses Paran the same way. The last words, מִימִינוֹ אֵשׁ דָּת לָמוֹ (mīmīnō ʾēsh dāt lāmō), are uncertain; 'fiery law' is one guess at them.

other_readings.reading: A poetic description of God appearing to give the Torah, picturing him approaching Israel from several directions. Rashi cites the tradition that God first offered the Torah to the peoples of Seir and Paran and they refused it.
A past event: God's appearance at Sinai with his angels. Jesus did not teach in Seir, which is Edom, south-east of Judea, and the wilderness of Paran lies in the Sinai region, not at Mecca.
An old poem about God marching from the southern desert, similar to Judges 5:4-5 and Habakkuk 3:3.

prophecies.status_reason: The verse is in the past tense, its subject is God rather than any prophet, and the three places are stops in Israel's own desert journey. The one real textual link is that Ishmael is said to have lived in the wilderness of Paran.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading, a past appearance of God to Israel, is the one the wording supports.

prophecies.title: Is Muhammad named in Song of Solomon 5:16?
prophecies.claim: The Hebrew of this verse contains the word 'maḥamaddim', which sounds like Muhammad with the plural ending '-im'. Muslims who use this argument say the ending is a plural of respect, as in 'Elohim', so the verse says 'he is Muhammad' and names the Prophet in the Hebrew Bible. They add that translators hid the name by translating it as 'altogether lovely'.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The verse reads חִכּוֹ מַמְתַקִּים וְכֻלּוֹ מַחֲמַדִּים (ḥikkō mamtaqqīm wᵉkhullō maḥămaddīm), 'his mouth is sweetness, and all of him is delights'. מַחֲמַדִּים is the plural of the common noun מַחְמָד (maḥmād), 'something desirable', from the root ḥ-m-d, 'to desire'; it stands in parallel with 'sweetnesses' in the same line. The same noun is used for Ezekiel's wife, 'the desire of your eyes' (Ezekiel 24:16), and for valuables (1 Kings 20:6, Lamentations 1:10). The speaker is a woman describing her lover's body part by part, from his head to his legs (5:10-16), to the daughters of Jerusalem.

other_readings.reading: A love poem, traditionally read as a picture of God and Israel. The word is an ordinary noun meaning 'delightful things'; if it were the name here it would have to be the name in the other verses where it appears.
The same: a common noun in a love song, sometimes read as a picture of Christ and the church. The Hebrew root means 'desire' while the Arabic root ḥ-m-d means 'praise'; the two only sound alike.
No scholar of Hebrew treats the word as a proper name. Translations have not hidden anything: 'lovely' or 'desirable' is what the word means everywhere it is used.

prophecies.status_reason: The word is a common Hebrew noun used elsewhere of a wife and of treasures, set in a woman's description of her lover's body. The resemblance to the name Muhammad is one of sound only.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish and Christian reading; the text gives no support to the claim.

prophecies.title: Is the servant of Isaiah 42 Muhammad?
prophecies.claim: Isaiah describes God's chosen servant who brings justice and a law to the nations, does not fail until he has established it on earth, and is a light to the Gentiles. Verse 11 then calls on the villages of Kedar and the people of Sela to sing. Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), so Muslims say the servant arises among the Arabs: Muhammad brought a law, defeated idolatry (42:8, 42:17) and did not die until his mission had succeeded, unlike Jesus, who established no law on earth.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: God presents עַבְדִּי (ʿavdī), 'my servant', on whom he puts his spirit, who 'will not shout nor raise his voice' in the street, will not break a bruised reed, and for whose teaching (תּוֹרָתוֹ, tōrātō) the coastlands wait. In 42:10-12 the whole earth is called to praise God: the sea, the coastlands, the desert, 'the villages that Kedar inhabits' and the people of Sela. Kedar is one item in that list of far-off places, and the servant is not said to come from there. The servant has been identified a chapter earlier as 'Israel, my servant' (41:8), and later in this same chapter he is blind and deaf (42:19).

other_readings.reading: The servant is Israel, as Isaiah 41:8 says and as Rashi explains here ('my servant Jacob'). Israel's task is to be a light to the nations; Kedar is named only as one of the distant peoples who will join the praise.
Matthew 12:17-21 quotes these verses about Jesus, pointing to his quiet and gentle manner. The spirit put on the servant is linked with Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:16).
The first of the 'servant songs'. In context the servant is Israel or an ideal figure standing for Israel; Kedar and Sela belong to a poem calling the ends of the earth to praise.

prophecies.status_reason: Kedar is in the text and Kedar is an Ishmaelite tribe, which is a real point. But Kedar appears in a list of distant places told to praise God, not as the servant's home, and the surrounding chapters name the servant as Israel. 'He will not shout nor raise his voice in the street' also fits poorly with a public preacher and commander.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading (the servant is Israel) has the most direct support in the surrounding text; the Christian and Muslim readings each apply it to a later figure.

prophecies.title: Is the Paraclete promised in John 14:16 Muhammad?
prophecies.claim: Jesus promised 'another' helper who would come after he left, guide people into all truth, and 'not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak'. Muslims say this describes a human prophet who recites what is revealed to him, as the Quran says of Muhammad (Quran 53:3-4), and that it is the Gospel side of Jesus's announcement of 'Ahmad' in Quran 61:6. Some add that the original Greek word was not paraklētos ('helper') but periklytos ('praised one'), which means the same as Ahmad.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The word is παράκλητος (paraklētos), 'one called alongside': an advocate, helper or comforter. No known Greek manuscript of John reads periklytos. The passages say who the Paraclete is: 'the Spirit of truth, whom the world can't receive, for it doesn't see him ... he lives with you and will be in you' (14:17), and 'the Counselor, the Holy Spirit' (14:26). He is sent by Jesus (16:7), to the disciples Jesus is talking to, and he will 'remind you of all that I said to you'. Acts 1:5 has Jesus say this will happen 'not many days from now', and Acts 2:1-4 describes it.

other_readings.reading: The Paraclete is the Holy Spirit, given to the disciples at Pentecost about fifty days later. A man born more than five centuries afterwards could not be 'with you forever', be 'in you', or be unseen by the world. 'Another' helper means another besides Jesus, who is himself called a paraklētos in 1 John 2:1.
Not a Jewish text, and Judaism takes no position on it. The idea of God's spirit resting on people is found in the Hebrew Bible.
The Paraclete sayings are John's way of describing the Spirit's presence in the community after Jesus. The periklytos proposal has no manuscript support.

prophecies.status_reason: The passage itself names the Paraclete as the Holy Spirit, says he is invisible to the world and lives inside the disciples, and says Jesus sends him to those same disciples. 'He will speak what he hears' is the only detail that suits a human prophet, and the claimed original word periklytos appears in no manuscript.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Christian reading; the text defines the Paraclete in terms that do not fit a human being.

prophecies.title: Did Jesus foretell a messenger named Ahmad (Quran 61:6)?
prophecies.claim: The Quran reports Jesus telling the Children of Israel that he confirms the Torah and brings good news of a messenger to come after him 'whose name is Ahmad'. Ahmad is a name of Muhammad, from the same root as Muhammad. Muslims say this is what Jesus actually taught, that traces of it survive in the Paraclete sayings of John, and that where the Gospels lack it they have been altered or are incomplete.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The Arabic is وَمُبَشِّرًۢا بِرَسُولٍ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِى ٱسْمُهُۥٓ أَحْمَدُ (wa-mubashshiran bi-rasūlin yaʾtī min baʿdī smuhu aḥmad), 'bringing good news of a messenger who comes after me, whose name is Ahmad'. أَحْمَدُ (aḥmad) is from the root ḥ-m-d, 'praise', and can be a proper name or a description, 'more praiseworthy'; Pickthall translates it 'the Praised One'. This is a statement in the Quran about what Jesus said; it is not a quotation from any earlier book. No saying like it is found in the four Gospels or the rest of the New Testament.

other_readings.reading: Jesus never says this in any Gospel. The helper he does promise is the Holy Spirit (John 14:26), and he warns of false prophets rather than announcing a further prophet. A report written six centuries later cannot be checked against any earlier source.
Not a Jewish text. The Hebrew Bible names no coming prophet called Ahmad or Muhammad.
Some connect the verse with the Paraclete sayings by way of the rare Greek word periklytos, 'renowned', but there is no manuscript evidence that John ever read that.

prophecies.status_reason: As a claim about what the Bible contains, there is no supporting text: no Gospel records Jesus naming a successor. The claim rests on the Quran's own authority, so it is convincing to those who already accept the Quran and cannot be confirmed from the earlier books.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: On the Gospel texts as they exist, the Christian reading; the Muslim claim depends on the Gospels having lost something, which the manuscripts do not show.

prophecies.title: Did the Quran predict the Roman victory over Persia (Quran 30:2-4)?
prophecies.claim: When Persia had crushed the Byzantine Romans and taken Jerusalem, the Quran announced that the Romans, after their defeat, would win within a few years. At the time this looked impossible, yet the emperor Heraclius reversed the war and defeated Persia. Muslims say this is a clear, dated prediction of a future event that came true, something a false prophet would never have risked.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: The text reads غُلِبَتِ ٱلرُّومُ (ghulibati r-rūm), 'the Romans have been defeated', 'in the nearest land', and then وَهُم مِّنۢ بَعْدِ غَلَبِهِمْ سَيَغْلِبُونَ (wa-hum min baʿdi ghalabihim sa-yaghlibūn), 'and they, after their defeat, will overcome', فِى بِضْعِ سِنِينَ (fī biḍʿi sinīn), 'within a few years'. بِضْع (biḍʿ) is a small number, traditionally three to nine; Sahih International translates 'within three to nine years' and Pickthall 'within ten years'. In history, Persia took Jerusalem in 614; Heraclius began winning in 622, won decisively at Nineveh in 627, and peace followed in 628.

other_readings.reading: The reversal did happen, but the timing is loose: from the fall of Jerusalem in 614 to the decisive victory in 627-628 is thirteen to fourteen years, more than 'three to nine'. The date the verses were first recited is known only from later Muslim tradition. A correct forecast of a war is not by itself proof of revelation.
Judaism has no stake in the verse. By the Torah's own test a true prediction is required of a prophet but is not enough on its own (Deuteronomy 18:22 with Deuteronomy 13:1-3).

Most accept the passage as early and as referring to the Persian war. Classical commentaries also record a minority reading with the vowels reversed ('the Romans have defeated ... they will be defeated'), which would point to a different event.

prophecies.status_reason: The text makes a plain, short-range prediction that a defeated empire would win, and it did. The open questions are outside the text: exactly when the verses were first recited, and which defeat and which victory the 'few years' are counted between.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Muslim reading is the plain sense of the words; whether a correct forecast proves prophethood is a separate question the text cannot settle.

prophecies.title: Has the world peace of Isaiah 2:4 come?
prophecies.claim: The prophets tie the messianic age to the end of war: nations will beat their swords into plowshares and stop learning war, and all peoples will come to Jerusalem to learn God's ways. Jews point out that no such age has arrived. War has continued without a break since the time of Jesus and since the time of Muhammad, so the Messiah the prophets describe has not yet come.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: Isaiah says that בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (bᵉʾaḥărīt hayyāmīm), 'in the latter days', the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised up, all nations will stream to it for teaching, and God 'will judge between the nations'. Then: לֹא־יִשָּׂא גוֹי אֶל־גּוֹי חֶרֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְדוּ עוֹד מִלְחָמָה (lōʾ yissāʾ gōy ʾel gōy ḥerev wᵉlōʾ yilmᵉdū ʿōd milḥāmāh), 'nation will not lift up sword against nation, neither will they learn war any more'. The same words appear in Micah 4:3. The passage does not mention a Messiah; God is the one who judges. Isaiah 11 is where the peace is linked to a king from David's line.

other_readings.reading: The peace is real but future: it comes when Jesus returns to rule. For now his kingdom spreads without force, and Jesus himself said his first coming would bring division (Matthew 10:34). Christians see nations coming to Israel's God as already begun.

Islam also looks ahead to a time of justice and peace near the end of the world, which hadith traditions connect with the return of Jesus; the Quran calls him a sign of the Hour (Quran 43:61). Muslims therefore agree it is still to come.
A vision of Jerusalem as the centre of a peaceful world, shared by Isaiah and Micah. It describes a hope, without a date or a named agent.

prophecies.status_reason: The text describes worldwide disarmament and the nations coming to Jerusalem for instruction, and that has plainly not happened. The limit on the claim is that this passage names no Messiah, so it shows the promised age has not come rather than saying who must bring it.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading that this is unfulfilled is what the text supports; Christians and Muslims agree it is still future and differ only on who brings it.

prophecies.title: Has Ezekiel 37:21-28 been fulfilled?
prophecies.claim: Ezekiel lists what happens when the Messiah reigns: all Israel is gathered from the nations to its land, the two kingdoms become one, a king from David rules them, they keep God's laws, and God's sanctuary stands among them forever so that the nations know God. Jews say these are public, checkable events and that none of them was completed by Jesus. A Messiah who has not done them has not yet done the Messiah's work.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: God says he will take the children of Israel from among the nations, make them 'one nation in the land', and that וְעַבְדִּי דָוִד מֶלֶךְ עֲלֵיהֶם (wᵉʿavdī dāwid melekh ʿălēhem), 'my servant David will be king over them', with 'one shepherd' for all. They will follow God's ordinances and statutes, live in the land forever, and God will set מִקְדָּשִׁי (miqdāshī), 'my sanctuary', among them forever. The result is stated: 'the nations will know that I am the LORD who sanctifies Israel'. Every item is something done to or in the nation of Israel in its land.

other_readings.reading: Jesus is the promised son of David (Luke 1:32-33) and the 'one shepherd' (John 10:16). The sanctuary is fulfilled in his own body (John 2:19-21) and in God's presence with his people (Revelation 21:22), and the full kingdom comes at his return.

Jesus is the Messiah in the Quran, but the Quran does not describe him ruling Israel from a rebuilt sanctuary. The Quran presents God's covenant with the Children of Israel as conditional on their keeping it (Quran 2:40).
A programme for the restoration of both kingdoms after the Babylonian exile under a new David. The modern return of Jews to the land matches the first item only.

prophecies.status_reason: The text names a Davidic king, a reunited Israel in its land, obedience to God's statutes and a permanent sanctuary. No king of David's line reigns there and no sanctuary stands, so on its plain terms it is unfulfilled.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading; the Christian reading requires taking the king, the land and the sanctuary in a spiritual sense or moving them to a second coming.

prophecies.title: Has the reign of the 'shoot of Jesse' in Isaiah 11 begun?
prophecies.claim: Isaiah 11 is the fullest portrait of the Messiah: a descendant of David's father Jesse, filled with God's spirit, who judges the poor fairly and destroys the wicked, in whose time the wolf lives with the lamb, the earth is full of the knowledge of God, and the scattered people of Israel and Judah are gathered from the four corners of the earth. Jews say none of the public results has appeared, so the one described has not yet come.
prophecies.what_the_text_says: וְיָצָא חֹטֶר מִגֵּזַע יִשָׁי (wᵉyātsāʾ ḥōṭer miggēzaʿ yishāy), 'a shoot will come out of the stump of Jesse': a new king from David's family after it has been cut down. The spirit of the LORD rests on him, he judges with righteousness, and 'with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked'. Then predators and prey live together, 'they will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD', the nations seek him (11:10), and God gathers 'the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' (11:12). The chapter runs these together as one period.

other_readings.reading: Jesus is the shoot of Jesse on whom the Spirit rested (Matthew 3:16), and Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 for the nations putting their hope in him (Romans 15:12). The peace among creatures and the full knowledge of God belong to his second coming.
Jesus is accepted as the Messiah, a human servant of God. The Quran does not describe this reign; Muslim tradition places a time of peace and justice at his return.
A hope for an ideal Davidic king, written when David's dynasty was weak or fallen. The animal scene pictures an end to violence.

prophecies.status_reason: The chapter describes a Davidic ruler together with the end of harm, universal knowledge of God and the gathering of the exiles. Christians can point to verse 10, nations seeking a son of Jesse, as having happened; the rest is plainly not yet the state of the world.
prophecies.makes_more_sense: The Jewish reading that the chapter is unfulfilled as a whole; the Christian reading divides it between two comings, a division the chapter itself does not make.
